analysis.one_liner: Gives debit card users the same fraud protections and faster refunds that credit card users get.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules banks follow when a debit card is used without permission. It would cut the time a bank has to put money back in your account after an error from ten days to seven, cap your out-of-pocket loss for unauthorized debit card use at $50 the way credit card law already does, and make the bank — not you — prove a disputed charge was legitimate. It was introduced by a Democrat and a Republican in April 2014 and was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who use debit cards — which for many households are the main way they spend money — gain faster refunds when a transaction goes wrong, a hard $50 limit on what they can lose to fraud, and a presumption that the bank has to prove a disputed charge was legitimate. Consumers would no longer bear the risk of proving they didn't make a charge.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Debit card users, especially low-income households

how_it_helps.text: Requires a bank to recredit a consumer's account within seven business days after being notified of an error in an electronic debit transaction, down from ten days, with a fraud exception the regulator can use.
Caps a consumer's liability for unauthorized use of a debit card at $50, and only under narrow conditions, matching protections credit card holders already have under the Fair Credit Billing Act.
Places the burden of proof on the card issuer to show a charge was authorized or that all conditions for holding the consumer liable were met.

Counts a consumer as having notified the bank when reasonable steps were taken to alert it, whether or not any particular bank employee actually received the information, closing an excuse banks could use to dispute a consumer's report.

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit unions that issue debit cards would absorb more fraud losses directly instead of passing them to cardholders, would process error claims faster, and would carry the burden of proving disputed charges were legitimate. Some of that cost could show up in account fees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and credit unions issuing debit cards

drawbacks.text: Shifting fraud losses from cardholders to issuers raises banks' costs, and banks could respond by raising account fees or tightening debit card approval, which would fall hardest on customers who have no alternative to a checking account.
Allowing regulators to waive the seven-day recredit deadline to protect against fraud leaves banks a channel to delay refunds in fraud-prone cases, so the speed guarantee is not absolute.

The bill amends a law that already gives consumers substantial protections, including zero liability under most card network rules in practice, so the practical gain for many consumers is smaller than the headline suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the bill is a clear win: a capped $50 loss, a faster refund clock, and the bank bearing the burden of proof all remove real financial risk from people who use debit cards because they have no credit card. The main honest cost is that banks would eat more fraud losses and might pass some of that on through fees; whether that eats the consumer gain depends on competition among banks, but no household would ever be on the hook for more than $50 in fraud, which is the difference that matters.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Warner introduced the bill on April 2, 2014, joined by Republican Sen. Mark Kirk.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The committee took no further action, and the bill received no floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit unions that issue debit cards are better off, because they keep the existing rules under which consumers bear more of the risk and burden in unauthorized-transaction disputes. Consumers who might have gotten a $50 cap and a faster refund got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Mark Warner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Consumer Debit Card Protection Act of 2014 in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Mark Kirk
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making its introduction bipartisan.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never took it up, leaving it without a markup or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only recorded support was bipartisan — one Democrat and one Republican — and no one is recorded opposing it, because it never advanced far enough for a vote.

industries.industry: Debit card issuing banks and credit unions
industries.note: The bill shifts unauthorized-transaction losses from consumers to issuers, caps what a bank can charge a cardholder at $50, and makes the bank prove a disputed charge was legitimate. Issuers benefit from the current rules, which leave consumers carrying more of the fraud risk, so their interest here ran against the bill's beneficiary: cardholders.
